lines.text: Chapter 1: What a recession is.
lines.say: Chapter one: what a recession is.

lines.text: In the US, recessions are dated by a small committee at the National Bureau of Economic Research, or NBER.
lines.say: In the US, recessions are dated by a small committee at the National Bureau of Economic Research, known as N B E R.

lines.text: Its definition: a significant decline in economic activity, spread across the economy, lasting more than a few months.
lines.say: Its definition is a significant decline in economic activity that's spread across the economy and lasts more than a few months.

lines.text: NBER judges that with three tests: depth, diffusion and duration. Depth is how far activity falls.
lines.say: N B E R judges that with three tests: depth, diffusion and duration. Depth is how far activity falls.

lines.text: Diffusion is how widely the drop spreads across the economy, not just one industry.
lines.say: Diffusion is how widely the drop spreads across the economy, not just one industry.

lines.text: Duration is how long it lasts. And an extreme reading on one test can make up for a weaker one.
lines.say: Duration is how long it lasts. And an extreme reading on one test can make up for a weaker one.

lines.text: Now, the famous rule of thumb: two quarters in a row of shrinking GDP. NBER says it doesn't use that rule.

lines.text: Most recessions do include two down quarters. But the 2001 recession didn't, according to NBER, and it still counted.
lines.say: Most recessions do include two down quarters. But the two thousand one recession didn't, according to N B E R, and it still counted.

lines.text: And 2022 had its two down quarters, but unemployment averaged just 3.6% that year. That's not broad pain.

lines.text: One more catch: NBER waits for solid, revised data, so it names recessions late.

lines.text: So what causes one? There's no single cause, but history keeps repeating four big triggers.
lines.say: So what causes one? There's no single cause, but history keeps repeating four big triggers.

lines.text: They share one engine. People and businesses spend less, so sales fall, so companies cut jobs.
lines.say: They share one engine. People and businesses spend less, so sales fall, so companies cut jobs.

lines.text: And people who lose their jobs spend even less. The loop feeds itself.
lines.say: And people who lose their jobs spend even less. The loop feeds itself.

lines.text: Trigger one: an oil shock. In late 1973, an Arab oil embargo pushed oil from $2.90 a barrel to $11.65 by January 1974.

lines.text: Energy costs jumped for families and businesses, and the economy shrank for 16 months.

lines.text: Chapter 4: The warning signs.
lines.say: Chapter four: the warning signs.

lines.text: Since recessions get named late, economists watch signals in real time. Here are two famous ones.
lines.say: Since recessions get named late, economists watch signals in real time. Here are two famous ones.

lines.text: First, the yield curve. Normally, a 10-year Treasury note pays more interest than a 3-month bill.

lines.text: Chapter 6: The recap.

lines.text: One: a recession is a broad, deep, lasting drop, and NBER names it late. Two shrinking quarters is just a rule of thumb.

post.yt_desc:
The Great Recession began in December 2007, but it wasn't made official until December 1, 2008. This video explains how the NBER defines and dates recessions (and why two shrinking GDP quarters, like those reported in 2022, is only a rule of thumb), every US recession since 1973 with its length, and the four triggers history keeps repeating: oil shocks, Fed tightening, bursting bubbles and sudden shocks. We cover the warning signs economists watch, the yield curve and the Sahm rule, including their 2022-2024 false alarms, then show what a recession does to jobs, interest rates, stocks and savings, with worked examples labeled as our own math. No predictions about the next recession.

CHAPTERS

Sources: NBER, US Business Cycle Expansions and Contractions and Business Cycle Dating FAQ; NBER Business Cycle Dating Committee announcements (Dec 1, 2008; June 8, 2020); BEA, GDP Q2 2022 third estimate (Sept 2022); BLS unemployment rate data (annual averages 1990-2025; monthly peaks), BLS Employment Situation, September 2026 (Oct 2026); BLS, payroll employment April 2020; Federal Reserve History, Recession of 1981-82; CNBC (2023) and New York Fed yield curve model; Claudia Sahm on the Sahm rule; NBC News and Confluence Investment Management on 1970s oil prices; S&P 500 and Nasdaq drawdown data. Worked examples are our own math with stated assumptions.

News and education, not financial advice.
